Playbook — Why PPC & Takt Discipline Win Projects

PPC and takt-rhythm monitoring aren't reporting overhead — they're the two instruments that tell you whether the production system is actually working. The theory behind them, and what separates teams who get the benefit from teams who just fill in the spreadsheet.

Why Track PPC

Percent Plan Complete isn't a productivity score — it's a reliability score. It only means something once you see it against the chain it comes from:

  • PPC measures promise-keeping, not output. A missed task usually means a broken commitment upstream — a constraint that was never actually cleared — not a slow crew. Blaming the trade for a planning failure is the single most common way to kill an LPS rollout.
  • It's a leading indicator. PPC flags trouble at the week level, long before it shows up as a blown milestone on the master programme. By the time a CPM schedule shows red, the damage is already done; PPC catches it while it's still cheap to fix.
  • The real value is in the Reasons for Variance, not the percentage. Every miss should carry a reason (see the Daily Log and 6-Week Look-Ahead tabs). Reasons that get counted and ranked — not just logged and forgotten — tell you exactly where the system is actually breaking.
  • Tracked over time, it shows whether your planning discipline is improving. A single week's PPC is a data point; the trend line is the real measure of a maturing Last Planner System.
< 50%

80%+

General reference ranges seen in Last Planner practice, not a fixed target — a team new to LPS often starts in the 30–50% band, and the goal is a rising trend, not an instant 80%.

Why Monitor the Takt Plan

A takt plan turns the whole site into one synchronised production line — every trade knows exactly which zone it's in and when it hands off, like wagons on a train moving through stations on a fixed rhythm. That only holds if someone is watching the rhythm.

  • A late wagon doesn't stay local — it cascades. A two-day slip in one zone pushes every trade behind it, in every zone after that, compounding as it travels down the line. This is exactly what the crossing lines on the Flowline tab are showing you when they appear.
  • The flowline is an early-warning instrument, not a record-keeping chart. Parallel, evenly-spaced diagonal bands mean a stable rhythm. Converging, crossing, or gapped bands mean a rhythm break is already in progress — catchable now, instead of discovered at week twelve.
  • Watching work-in-progress keeps the site from sliding back into "start everywhere, finish nowhere." That's the exact failure mode of trade-stacked, un-sequenced construction that takt planning exists to solve — limiting active zones to what the crews can actually hold a rhythm across.
  • Monitoring feeds the Look-Ahead, not the other way round. Watching the plan is what tells you which constraints need clearing three, four, five weeks out — before the wagon arrives and finds the track still blocked.

How to Be Successful Managing This Phase

Eight things that separate a Last Planner System that actually changes site behaviour from one that's just a compliance exercise.

1
Make the look-ahead do real work

Screen every constraint — design info, materials, prerequisite work, space, crew, equipment — before a task is allowed into the Weekly Work Plan. A committed task should already be constraint-free, not a hope that it will be.

2
Let the last planners plan

Foremen and trade supervisors — not just the scheduler — should be the ones making the weekly commitments. They're the ones who can actually see the constraints on the ground.

3
Review PPC together, without blame

It's a team diagnostic, not a scorecard for punishing a trade. The moment it's used to assign blame, people start sandbagging commitments to protect their numbers — and the data stops being honest.

4
Chase the reasons, not the percentage

Rank the Reasons for Variance, find the recurring root cause, and assign an owner to fix the system issue behind it. A late-delivering supplier will cost you every single week until someone actually owns fixing it.

5
Treat a stalled zone like a stopped line

In Lean manufacturing a line stoppage gets escalated immediately. A late wagon deserves the same urgency — not a shrug and a hope it catches up next week, by which point it's cascaded into three more zones.

6
Keep zones balanced

Takt only holds together if the work content per zone is roughly even across trades. A badly unbalanced zone forces either idle crews or crashed work — either one breaks the rhythm for everyone behind it.

7
Plan your buffers, don't discover them

A deliberate time buffer or a flex crew, placed where the plan is thinnest, absorbs the normal variability of a live site. Finding out you needed one mid-crisis is the expensive way to learn this.

8
Make the plan visible to everyone

A flowline or takt board only works as a management tool if the whole team can read it — on a screen in the site office, not buried in a spreadsheet only the planner opens. That's what this board is for.

SOP — Daily Log, History & Takt Plan Edits

How to keep the board current and build a reliable historical record, since there's no server behind this — the Excel file you export is the shared record, and the shared Drive folder is the sync mechanism.

In-app step (any tab)
Excel / Google Drive step
Decision point
Start / end of a session

Why dated files = history

No extra discipline required.

The Export button already names the file with today's date (SKN4C49_PPC_Log_YYYY-MM-DD.xlsx). Drop every export into the same shared Drive folder without renaming it, and the folder itself becomes a day-by-day archive — sort by name or date to open any past day's exact state. You don't need to rely on Drive's separate version-history feature for this to work, though it's a useful second safety net if your workspace keeps it.

Watch out for

This board has no live multi-user sync — the file is the sync.
  • One editor at a time. If two people import, edit, and export around the same time, whoever uploads last wins — the other person's changes are silently lost. Agree who "owns" the file for a given session.
  • Import before you edit if you're not certain you have the newest copy — especially on a different computer, or first thing in a shift.
  • Site Status vs Daily Log status are tracked separately by design (see the Time-Chainage Grid and Daily Log tabs) — update both if both are relevant to what happened.

Changing the Takt Plan

The issued programme is the starting point, not a fixed constraint — zones and individual activities can be resequenced two ways. Both update the whole board immediately: Flowline, Zone Map, Time-Chainage Grid, Dashboard, Look-Ahead.

Method 1 — Edit directly in the app

Fastest for a single change. No Excel involved.
  1. Move a whole zone — on the Flowline tab, click the zone's name in the left "Zone / Wagon" column (or on Dashboard, click its bar under Zone Durations). Pick a new start date → Move zone here. Every activity in that zone shifts together, keeping its own durations.
  2. Edit one activity — on the Flowline tab, click any individual coloured segment (not the zone name — the bar itself). Set a new start date and/or duration in working days → Apply to this activity. Only that activity and whatever follows it in the same zone shifts; everything earlier in that zone stays put.
  3. Undo one change — reopen the same zone or activity; a Reset this zone / Reset this activity button appears once something's been edited.
  4. Undo everything — Daily Log tab → ↺ Reset Schedule reverts every zone and activity to the originally issued programme dates.

Method 2 — Edit via Excel

Best for planning offline, or proposing a resequencing to the team before committing it.
  1. Export — Daily Log tab → ⬇ Export Excel.
  2. Open the "Zone Schedule" sheet — one row per zone, with its current start/end dates already filled in.
  3. Fill in "New Start Date" for any zone you want to move — leave every other zone's cell blank. This sheet only moves whole zones; edit individual activities in the app itself (Method 1).
  4. Re-import — Daily Log tab → ⬆ Import Excel → pick the edited file. The app rebuilds that zone's activity chain from the new date, same durations, Sundays skipped.
  5. Verify — export again and check the "Resequenced?" column: it flags exactly which zones have been moved and whether individual activities inside them were also touched.
What does — and doesn't — move automatically: a schedule edit only shifts the zone or activity you touched (and, for an activity edit, whatever comes after it in that same zone). Nothing cascades to other zones, even ones that were takt-chained to it in the original plan — if stretching Excavation in Part A1 should logically push Part A2 as well, that's on you to go make that edit too. This is deliberate: auto-cascading a whole schedule silently is a good way to hide a real problem. Check the Flowline's crossing lines and the Dashboard's "Peak Concurrent Zones" after any edit — that's the tool's way of showing you when a resequencing creates an overlap or a gap.
